USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold our tariff posture and go to the G20 in Buenos Aires to press for a substantive deal, keeping the scheduled January 1 rise to 25% on $200B — and the threatened $257B tranche — as credible leverage rather than pulling the trigger now. Do not escalate further before the summit, and do not concede structural IP/tech-transfer demands without a matching commitment from Beijing. Treat the Xi meeting as the pressure-release valve that lets us convert our leverage into purchases and enforcement without imposing costlier consumer-facing tariffs.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is material but not existential. We have already tariffed ~$250B of Chinese goods, with the $200B tranche set to jump from 10% to 25% on Jan 1, 2019 and another ~$257B threatened if talks fail (event timeline 2018-09-17/09-18/09-24; BI 2018-11-01). The real-economy bite is real: soybean prices are down ~20% and China has effectively shut out the US from its top soy market, eroding ~$20B of ag exports and pressuring the farm belt ahead of a $12B bailout (McClatchy 2018-11-03; Politico 2018-10-23). Macro shows growth holding — industrial production up (104.1), consumer sentiment elevated (~97.5), CPI contained — but stress is building: the 10Y-2Y spread has flattened (3.22% vs 2.96%) and Baa corporate yields widened to 5.18%, signs the escalation is beginning to tighten credit and feed market anxiety (country_health). Escalating now would raise US consumer prices, feed the Fed's tightening, and could invite deeper China retaliation that hits farmers again — while Trump's own Nov 1 call with Xi and the scheduled G20 meeting (timeline 2018-11-01) show both sides are signaling a deal is possible. That is why the action stance is moderate de-escalation-adjacent (negotiate/hold): the leverage is best cashed in at the negotiating table, keeping the 25% rise and $257B threat as the credible stick rather than executing them prematurely.
key_factors: ~$250B of Chinese imports already tariffed; $200B scheduled to rise 10%→25% on Jan 1, 2019
~$257B additional tranche threatened if G20 talks fail
Soybean prices down ~20%; China shut out of ~$20B of US ag exports; $12B farmer bailout
Nov 1 Trump-Xi phone call and scheduled G20 meeting = window for a deal
US economy still solid (IP up, sentiment ~97.5, CPI contained) but credit widening (Baa 5.18%) and a flattening yield curve signal building stress
Dollar strong (broad index up ~4.4%) — no FX pressure on the US

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump directs USTR to finalize List 3: 10% tariffs on ~$200B of Chinese imports effective Sept 24, scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.
Trump and Xi hold a phone call focused on trade; agree to meet at the G20 in Argentina.
Moody's Baa corporate bond yield rose from 4.81% (May) to 5.18% (Nov 7) — credit conditions tightening.
Soybean prices fell by about 20% after the tariffs were enacted... Trump announced a $12 billion bailout for farmers.
Soybean prices down roughly $2/bushel or 20%; US growers effectively shut out of the world's largest soy market in China.
The Trump administration is readying tariffs on all remaining Chinese goods... an additional $257 billion worth of Chinese imports.
